docs.title: numerax
docs.text: Statistical and numerical computation functions for JAX, focusing on tools not available in the main JAX API.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This package provides JAX-compatible implementations of specialized numerical functions with full differentiability support. All functions are designed to work seamlessly with JAX's transformations (JIT, grad, vmap, etc.) and follow JAX's functional programming paradigms.

docs.title: Special Functions (numerax.special)
docs.text: Mathematical special functions with custom derivative implementations. Functions provide exact gradients through custom JVP rules where standard automatic differentiation would be inefficient or unstable.

docs.title: Statistical Methods (numerax.stats)
docs.text: Advanced statistical computation tools for inference problems. Implements complex statistical models that benefit from JAX's compilation and differentiation capabilities.

docs.title: Utilities (numerax.utils)
docs.text: Development utilities for creating JAX-compatible functions with proper documentation support. Includes decorators and helpers for preserving function metadata when using JAX's advanced features like custom derivatives.

docs.title: erfcinv
docs.text:
erfcinv(x: ArrayLike) -> ArrayLike

Inverse complementary error function.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Computes the inverse of the complementary error function, finding \(y\) such that \(\text{erfc}(y) = x\) for given \(x \in (0, 2)\).

docs.title: Mathematical Background
docs.text:
The inverse complementary error function is related to the inverse error function by:

\[\text{erfcinv}(x) = \text{erfinv}(1 - x)\]

This relationship allows us to implement erfcinv as a simple wrapper around the existing JAX implementation of erfinv.

docs.title: Args
docs.text: • x: Input values in \((0, 2)\). Can be scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Values \(y\) where \(\text{erfc}(y) = x\).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numerax

# Single value
y = numerax.special.erfcinv(0.5)  # ≈ 0.4769

# Array input
x_vals = jnp.array([0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 1.9])
y_vals = numerax.special.erfcinv(x_vals)

# Differentiable for optimization
grad_fn = jax.grad(numerax.special.erfcinv)
sensitivity = grad_fn(0.5)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Differentiable: Full automatic differentiation support through JAX
  • Broadcasting: Supports JAX array broadcasting
  • Domain: Input must be in \((0, 2)\) for real outputs
  • Performance: JIT-compiled compatibility

docs.title: gammap_inverse
docs.text:
gammap_inverse(p: ArrayLike, a: float) -> ArrayLike

Inverse of the regularized incomplete gamma function.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Computes the inverse of the regularized incomplete gamma function, finding \(x\) such that \(P(a, x) = p\), where \(P(a, x)\) is the regularized incomplete gamma function. This is equivalent to computing quantiles of the \(\text{Gamma}(a, 1)\) distribution. The general strategy and the initial guess are based on the methods described in Numerical Recipes (Press et al., 2007).

docs.title: Mathematical Background
docs.text:
The regularized incomplete gamma function is defined as:

\[P(a, x) = \frac{\gamma(a, x)}{\Gamma(a)} = \frac{1}{\Gamma(a)} \int_0^x t^{a-1} e^{-t} dt\]

This function solves the inverse problem:

\[x = P^{-1}(a, p) \quad \text{such that} \quad P(a, x) = p\]

For a random variable \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a, 1)\), this gives:

\[x = F^{-1}(p) \quad \text{where} \quad F(x) = P(\Gamma(a), x)\]

docs.title: Numerical Method
docs.text:
Uses Halley's method for fast quadratic convergence:

\[x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{2f(x_n)f'(x_n)}{2[f'(x_n)]^2 - f(x_n)f''(x_n)}\]

where \(f(x) = P(a, x) - p\).

Initial guess based on Numerical Recipes (Press et al., 2007): - For \(a > 1\): Wilson-Hilferty approximation - For \(a \leq 1\): Asymptotic expansions

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• p: Probability values in \([0, 1]\). Can be scalar or array.
  • a: Shape parameter (must be positive). Scalar value.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Quantiles \(x\) where \(P(a, x) = p\). Same shape as input p.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numerax

# Single quantile
x = numerax.special.gammap_inverse(0.5, 2.0)  # Median of Gamma(2, 1)

# Multiple quantiles
p_vals = jnp.array([0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9])
x_vals = numerax.special.gammap_inverse(p_vals, 3.0)

# Verify inverse relationship
from jax.scipy.special import gammainc

p_recovered = gammainc(2.0, x)  # Should equal original p

# Differentiable for optimization
grad_fn = jax.grad(numerax.special.gammap_inverse)
sensitivity = grad_fn(0.5, 2.0)  # ∂x/∂p at median

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Convergence: Typically converges in 3-8 iterations
  • Differentiable: Custom JVP implementation using implicit function theorem
  • Domain: \(p \in [0, 1]\) and \(a > 0\)

docs.title: References
docs.text: Press, W. H., Teukolsky, S. A., Vetterling, W. T., & Flannery, B. P. (2007). Numerical Recipes: The Art of Scientific Computing (3rd ed.). Cambridge University Press.

docs.title: iv
docs.text:
iv(v: ArrayLike, z: ArrayLike) -> ArrayLike

Modified Bessel function of the first kind, real order.

Computes \(I_v(z)\) for real \(v\) and real \(z \ge 0\). This is a thin wrapper over ive:

\[I_v(z) = e^{z} \cdot \mathtt{ive}(v, z).\]

For large \(z\) (\(z \gtrsim 709\) in float64), \(\exp(z)\) overflows and this function returns +inf. Use ive directly when working with large arguments.

Matches the signature of scipy.special.iv, except that the out= parameter is not supported (JAX arrays are immutable). Differentiation w.r.t. z is provided by the underlying ive custom JVP; differentiating w.r.t. v raises TypeError.

docs.title: ive
docs.text:
ive(v: ArrayLike, z: ArrayLike) -> ArrayLike

Exponentially scaled modified Bessel function of the first kind.

Computes \(ive(v, z) = e^{-z} I_v(z)\) for real order \(v\) and real \(z \ge 0\). Unlike \(I_v(z)\), this scaled form stays finite for large \(z\) (decays like \(1/\sqrt{2\pi z}\)), so it is the numerically preferred primitive in likelihoods and probability densities.

Three regimes are evaluated in parallel and selected per element via jnp.where:

  • \(z < 30\): log-space power series (DLMF 10.25.2).
  • \(z \ge 30\) and \(v \ge 10\): Olver uniform asymptotic for large order (DLMF 10.41.3).
  • \(z \ge 30\) and \(v < 10\): Hankel large-argument asymptotic for fixed order (DLMF 10.40.1).

The thresholds (_SERIES_Z_THRESHOLD = 30.0, _OLVER_V_THRESHOLD = 10.0) are calibrated empirically against scipy.special.ive on a \((v, z)\) grid; the procedure lives in scripts/calibrate_bessel.py.

docs.text: Where each regime has relative error below 1e-7 vs. scipy.special.ive:

docs.title: Combined ive relative error
docs.text: The dispatched result, with threshold lines overlaid for direct comparison against the data-derived regions above:

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• v: real order. Scalar or array.
  • z: argument; must be real and >= 0. Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Scaled Bessel values; broadcast of the inputs.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Differentiable: custom JVP w.r.t. z only, using the recurrence \(I_v'(z) = (I_{v-1}(z) + I_{v+1}(z))/2\) (DLMF 10.29.1). Gradient w.r.t. v is not implemented; attempting to differentiate w.r.t. v raises TypeError rather than returning a silently-wrong value.
  • JIT/vmap: regime selection is via jnp.where, no Python control flow on data.
  • Accuracy target: ~1e-6 relative vs. scipy.special.ive for v >= 0, z > 0.

docs.title: numerax.stats
docs.text: Statistics submodule for numerax.

docs.title: make_profile_llh
docs.text:
make_profile_llh(llh_fn: Callable, is_nuisance: list[bool] | ndarray, get_initial_nuisance: Callable, tol: float = 1e-06, initial_value: float = 1e-09, initial_diff: float = 1000000000.0, optimizer: GradientTransformation = _DEFAULT_OPTIMIZER) -> Callable

Factory function for creating profile likelihood functions.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Profile likelihood is a statistical technique used when dealing with nuisance parameters that are not of primary interest but are necessary for the model. This function creates an optimized profile likelihood that maximizes over nuisance parameters while keeping inference parameters fixed.

docs.title: Mathematical Background
docs.text:
Given a likelihood function \(L(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\lambda})\) where \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) are parameters of interest and \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) are nuisance parameters, the profile likelihood is:

\[L_p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \max_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}} L(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\lambda})\]

In practice, we work with the log-likelihood \(\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\lambda}) = \log L(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\lambda})\):

\[\ell_p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \max_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}} \ell(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\lambda})\]

This function uses L-BFGS optimization to find the maximum likelihood estimates of nuisance parameters for each fixed value of inference parameters.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• llh_fn: Log likelihood function taking (params, *args) and returning scalar log likelihood value
  • is_nuisance: Boolean array where True indicates nuisance parameters and False indicates inference parameters
  • get_initial_nuisance: Function taking (*args) and returning initial values for nuisance parameters
  • tol: Convergence tolerance for the optimization (default: 1e-6)
  • initial_value: Initial objective value for convergence tracking (default: 1e-9)
  • initial_diff: Initial difference for convergence tracking (default: 1e9)
  • optimizer: Optax optimizer to use for maximization (default: lbfgs()). Currently tested only with the default L-BFGS optimizer

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Profile likelihood function with signature: (inference_values, *args) -> (profile_llh_value, optimal_nuisance, convergence_diff, num_iterations)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Consider fitting a normal distribution where we want to infer the mean \(\mu\) but treat the variance \(\sigma^2\) as a nuisance parameter:

import jax.numpy as jnp
import numerax

# Sample data
data = jnp.array([1.2, 0.8, 1.5, 0.9, 1.1, 1.3, 0.7, 1.4])


# Log likelihood for normal distribution
def normal_llh(params, data):
    mu, log_sigma = params  # Use log(sigma) for numerical stability
    sigma = jnp.exp(log_sigma)
    return jnp.sum(
        -0.5 * jnp.log(2 * jnp.pi)
        - log_sigma
        - 0.5 * ((data - mu) / sigma) ** 2
    )


# Profile over log_sigma (nuisance), infer mu
is_nuisance = [False, True]  # mu=inference, log_sigma=nuisance


def get_initial_log_sigma(data):
    # Initialize with log of sample standard deviation
    return jnp.array([jnp.log(jnp.std(data))])


profile_llh = numerax.stats.make_profile_llh(
    normal_llh, is_nuisance, get_initial_log_sigma
)

# Evaluate profile likelihood at different mu values
mu_test = 1.0
llh_val, opt_log_sigma, diff, n_iter = profile_llh(
    jnp.array([mu_test]), data
)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The function is JIT-compiled for performance
  • Uses L-BFGS optimization which is well-suited for smooth likelihood surfaces
  • Returns convergence information for diagnostics
  • Handles parameter masking automatically
  • Consider using log-parameterization for positive parameters (e.g., \(\log \sigma\)) for unconstrained optimization
  • This function might not work well if the likelihood surface has multiple local maxima; in such cases, consider ensuring that initial guesses are close to the global maximum.

docs.title: chi2
docs.text:
Chi-squared distribution functions.

This module provides a complete interface for chi-squared distribution computations, combining re-exported JAX's standard statistical functions (pdf, cdf, etc.) with a custom high-precision percent point function (ppf).

All functions support location-scale parameterization and are fully compatible with JAX transformations (JIT, grad, vmap).

docs.title: ppf
docs.text:
ppf(q: ArrayLike, df: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Chi-squared percent point function (inverse CDF).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Computes the percent point function (quantile function) of the chi-squared distribution. This is the inverse of the cumulative distribution function, finding \(x\) such that \(P(X \leq x) = q\) for a chi-squared random variable \(X\) with \(\text{df}\) degrees of freedom.

docs.title: Mathematical Background
docs.text:
The chi-squared distribution with \(\text{df}\) degrees of freedom is a special case of the gamma distribution:

\[X \sim \chi^2(\text{df}) \equiv \text{Gamma}\left( \frac{\text{df}}{2}, 2\right)\]

For the location-scale family:

\[Y = \text{loc} + \text{scale} \cdot X\]

The percent point function is computed as:

\[ \text{ppf}(q, \text{df}, \text{loc}, \text{scale}) = \text{loc} + \text{scale} \cdot 2 \cdot \text{gammap\_inverse}\left(q, \frac{\text{df}}{2}\right) \]

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• q: Probability values in \([0, 1]\). Can be scalar or array.
  • df: Degrees of freedom (must be positive). Can be scalar or array.
  • loc: Location parameter (default: 0). Can be scalar or array.
  • scale: Scale parameter (must be positive, default: 1). Can be scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Quantiles \(x\) where \(P(X \leq x) = q\). Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numerax

# Single quantile
x = numerax.stats.chi2.ppf(0.5, df=2)  # Median of χ²(2)

# Multiple quantiles
q_vals = jnp.array([0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9])
x_vals = numerax.stats.chi2.ppf(q_vals, df=3)

# Location-scale family
x_scaled = numerax.stats.chi2.ppf(0.5, df=2, loc=1, scale=2)

# Differentiable for optimization
grad_fn = jax.grad(numerax.stats.chi2.ppf)
sensitivity = grad_fn(0.5, 2.0)  # ∂x/∂q at median

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Differentiable: Automatic differentiation through gammap_inverse
  • Broadcasting: Supports JAX array broadcasting for all parameters
  • Performance: JIT-compiled compatibility

docs.title: halfnorm
docs.text:
Half-normal distribution functions.

This module provides the density, distribution, and quantile functions of the half-normal distribution (the distribution of \(|Z|\) for a standard normal \(Z\)), which JAX does not provide. The signatures mirror scipy.stats.halfnorm (including loc and scale), each function is evaluated in a form that stays accurate in the tails in both float32 and float64, and all functions are compatible with JAX transformations (JIT, grad, vmap).

docs.title: cdf
docs.text:
cdf(x: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Half-normal cumulative distribution function.

Computes \(\text{erf}(y/\sqrt{2})\) for \(y = (x - \text{loc})/\text{scale} \ge 0\), and zero below the support. Using erf rather than \(2\Phi(y) - 1\) keeps full relative accuracy for \(y\) near zero. See logpdf for the mathematical background.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• x: Quantile values. Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location parameter (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale: Scale parameter (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Cumulative probabilities. Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: isf
docs.text:
isf(q: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Half-normal inverse survival function.

Computes \(-\Phi^{-1}(q/2)\), i.e. ppf(1 - q) without forming \(1 - q\), so upper-tail quantiles for tiny \(q\) stay accurate, then applies \(\text{loc} + \text{scale} \cdot (\cdot)\). Returns inf at \(q = 0\), loc at \(q = 1\), and nan outside \([0, 1]\). See logpdf for the mathematical background.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• q: Survival probabilities in \([0, 1]\). Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location parameter (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale: Scale parameter (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Quantiles \(x\) where \(P(X > x) = q\). Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: logcdf
docs.text:
logcdf(x: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Half-normal log cumulative distribution function.

Computes \(\log \text{erf}(y/\sqrt{2})\) for small \(y\) and \(\text{log1p}(-\text{erfc}(y/\sqrt{2}))\) for \(y \ge 1\), where \(y = (x - \text{loc})/\text{scale}\), so that neither regime loses precision. Returns -inf for \(y \le 0\). See logpdf for the mathematical background.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• x: Quantile values. Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location parameter (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale: Scale parameter (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Log cumulative probabilities. Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: logpdf
docs.text:
logpdf(x: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Half-normal log probability density function.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Computes the natural logarithm of the probability density function of the half-normal distribution in the location-scale family.

docs.title: Mathematical Background
docs.text:
The half-normal distribution is the distribution of \(X = |Z|\) for \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\). Its standard (\(\text{loc}=0\), \(\text{scale}=1\)) density on the support \(x \ge 0\) is

\[f(x) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\, e^{-x^2/2},\]

with distribution and survival functions

\[F(x) = \text{erf}\!\left(\tfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\right), \qquad S(x) = \text{erfc}\!\left(\tfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 2\,\Phi(-x),\]

where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF. The quantile function is \(F^{-1}(q) = \sqrt{2}\,\text{erfinv}(q) = -\Phi^{-1}\!\left( \tfrac{1 - q}{2}\right)\).

The location-scale family follows the usual convention \(f(x; \text{loc}, \text{scale}) = \tfrac{1}{\text{scale}} f\!\left( \tfrac{x - \text{loc}}{\text{scale}}\right)\).

Every function in this module evaluates whichever of the equivalent forms is accurate in the relevant regime: cdf uses erf (full relative accuracy near the origin) and sf uses erfc (relative accuracy in the upper tail); logsf switches to an asymptotic expansion so it stays accurate far past where erfc underflows; ppf switches between erfinv and ndtri at \(q = 1/2\) so that neither tiny \(q\) nor \(q\) close to one loses precision; and isf evaluates \(-\Phi^{-1}(q/2)\) directly rather than forming \(1 - q\).

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• x: Quantile values. Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location parameter (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale: Scale parameter (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Log probability density values. Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numerax

# Single value
lp = numerax.stats.halfnorm.logpdf(1.0)

# Vectorized, with location and scale
x_vals = jnp.array([0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0])
lps = numerax.stats.halfnorm.logpdf(x_vals, loc=0.0, scale=2.0)

# Differentiable in x, loc, and scale
grad_fn = jax.grad(numerax.stats.halfnorm.logpdf, argnums=2)
sensitivity = grad_fn(1.0, 0.0, 2.0)  # d logpdf / d scale

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Differentiable: w.r.t. x, loc, and scale (and q for ppf/isf). Branch selections use safe substitutes so gradients (and second derivatives) stay NaN-free at finite points. At \(x = \text{loc}\), cdf, sf and logsf return the one-sided (right) derivative.
  • Precision: results follow the input dtype. Accuracy is close to machine precision in both float32 and float64; far in the upper tail sf and pdf are limited by the conditioning of \(e^{-y^2/2}\), about \(y^2\) ulps.
  • Broadcasting: Supports JAX array broadcasting for all parameters.
  • Support boundary: for \(x < \text{loc}\) the density is zero (logpdf returns -inf), matching scipy.stats.halfnorm. \(x = \text{loc}\) is in the support, where the density is \(\sqrt{2/\pi}/\text{scale}\). nan inputs propagate to nan.

docs.title: logsf
docs.text:
logsf(x: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Half-normal log survival function.

Evaluates \(\log S(y)\) for \(y = (x - \text{loc})/\text{scale}\) in three regimes: \(\text{log1p}(-\text{erf}(y/\sqrt{2}))\) for \(y < 1\), \(\log \text{erfc}(y/\sqrt{2})\) for \(1 \le y < y_t\), and beyond that the asymptotic expansion

\[\log S(y) = \tfrac12 \log\tfrac{2}{\pi} - \tfrac{y^2}{2} - \log y + \log\!\left(1 + \sum_{k=1}^{10} \frac{(-1)^k (2k-1)!!}{y^{2k}} \right).\]

The switch \(y_t\) is 20 in float64 and 8 in float32, before erfc (or the erfc**2 formed by second derivatives) underflows; the truncation error there is far below machine epsilon. Returns zero for \(y \le 0\). See logpdf for the mathematical background.

This is more accurate than $\log 2 + $ jax.scipy.special.log_ndtr \((-y)\), whose asymptotic branch loses ~1e-11 relative accuracy in the value (~1e-9 in the gradient) around \(y = 20\).

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• x: Quantile values. Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location parameter (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale: Scale parameter (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Log survival probabilities. Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: pdf
docs.text:
pdf(x: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Half-normal probability density function.

Computes \(\sqrt{2/\pi}\, e^{-y^2/2} / \text{scale}\) for \(y = (x - \text{loc})/\text{scale} \ge 0\), and zero below the support. This is exp(logpdf(...)); see logpdf for the full mathematical background and conventions.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• x: Quantile values. Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location parameter (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale: Scale parameter (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Probability density values. Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: ppf
docs.text:
ppf(q: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Half-normal percent point function (inverse CDF).

Computes \(\sqrt{2}\,\text{erfinv}(q)\) for \(q < 1/2\) and \(-\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\tfrac{1 - q}{2}\right)\) for \(q \ge 1/2\), then applies \(\text{loc} + \text{scale} \cdot (\cdot)\). The first form keeps tiny \(q\) from being rounded away; in the second, \(1 - q\) is exact. Returns loc at \(q = 0\), inf at \(q = 1\), and nan outside \([0, 1]\). See logpdf for the mathematical background.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• q: Probability values in \([0, 1]\). Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location parameter (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale: Scale parameter (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Quantiles \(x\) where \(P(X \leq x) = q\). Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: sf
docs.text:
sf(x: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Half-normal survival function (\(1 - \text{cdf}\)).

Computes \(\text{erfc}(y/\sqrt{2})\) for \(y = (x - \text{loc})/\text{scale} \ge 0\), and one below the support. This keeps relative accuracy in the upper tail (rather than computing \(1 - \text{cdf}\)), up to the inherent conditioning of about \(y^2\) ulps for large \(y\). See logpdf for the mathematical background.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• x: Quantile values. Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location parameter (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale: Scale parameter (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Survival probabilities. Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: ncx2
docs.text:
Non-central chi-squared distribution functions.

This module provides the probability density function (pdf) and its logarithm (logpdf) for the non-central chi-squared distribution, built on the numerically stable scaled modified Bessel function ive. The signatures mirror scipy.stats.ncx2 (including loc and scale), and all functions are compatible with JAX transformations (JIT, grad, vmap).

docs.title: logpdf
docs.text:
logpdf(x: ArrayLike, df: ArrayLike, nc: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Non-central chi-squared log probability density function.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Computes the natural logarithm of the probability density function of the non-central chi-squared distribution with \(\text{df}\) degrees of freedom and non-centrality parameter \(\lambda\) (nc), in the location-scale family.

docs.title: Mathematical Background
docs.text:
The non-central chi-squared distribution is the distribution of the sum of squares of \(k\) independent unit-variance normal random variables with means \(\mu_1, \ldots, \mu_k\):

\[X = \sum_{i=1}^{k} (Z_i + \mu_i)^2, \qquad Z_i \sim N(0, 1),\]

with degrees of freedom \(k = ext{df}\) and non-centrality parameter \(\lambda = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \mu_i^2\). Note that nc is \(\lambda\) itself (matching scipy.stats.ncx2), not \(\lambda^2\).

The standard (\( ext{loc}=0\), \( ext{scale}=1\)) density is

\[f(x; k, \lambda) = frac12 e^{-(x + \lambda)/2} \left( frac{x}{\lambda} ight)^{ u/2} I_{ u}\!\left(\sqrt{\lambda x} ight), \qquad u = frac{k}{2} - 1,\]

where \(I_{ u}\) is the modified Bessel function of the first kind. Using \(I_{ u}(z) = e^{z}\,\mathtt{ive}( u, z)\) and combining the exponentials via \(-(x+\lambda)/2 + \sqrt{\lambda x} = - frac12(\sqrt{x} - \sqrt{\lambda})^2\) gives the numerically stable form actually evaluated:

\[f = frac12\, e^{- rac12(\sqrt{x} - \sqrt{\lambda})^2} \left( frac{x}{\lambda} ight)^{ u/2} \mathtt{ive}\!\left( u, \sqrt{\lambda x} ight).\]

For small \(u = \lambda x / 4 < 1\) the factors \((x/\lambda)^{ u/2}\) and \(I_ u\) each vary like \(\lambda^{\mp u/2}\) and would cancel numerically (badly so in the gradient w.r.t. \(\lambda\) as \(\lambda o 0\)). There the power series of \(I_ u\) is used instead, in which that cancellation is exact:

\[\log f = -\log 2 - frac{x + \lambda}{2} + u \log frac{x}{2} - \log\Gamma( u + 1) + \log \sum_{k \ge 0} rac{u^k}{k!\,( u + 1)_k}.\]

The location-scale family follows the usual convention \(f(x; ext{loc}, ext{scale}) = frac{1}{ ext{scale}} f_{ ext{std}}\!\left( frac{x - ext{loc}}{ ext{scale}} ight)\).

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• x: Quantile values. Scalar or array.
  • df: Degrees of freedom (must be positive). Scalar or array.
  • nc: Non-centrality parameter \(\lambda \ge 0\). Scalar or array. nc == 0 reduces to the central chi-squared distribution.
  • loc: Location parameter (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale: Scale parameter (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Log probability density values. Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numerax

# Single value
lp = numerax.stats.ncx2.logpdf(4.0, df=3.0, nc=2.0)

# Vectorized
x_vals = jnp.array([0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0])
lps = numerax.stats.ncx2.logpdf(x_vals, df=3.0, nc=2.0)

# Differentiable in x and nc
grad_fn = jax.grad(numerax.stats.ncx2.logpdf, argnums=2)
sensitivity = grad_fn(4.0, 3.0, 2.0)  # d logpdf / d nc

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Differentiable: w.r.t. x, nc, loc, and scale. Not differentiable w.r.t. df -- df feeds the order of the underlying ive, which has no order-derivative, so differentiating w.r.t. df raises TypeError rather than returning a silently-wrong value.
  • Gradient at \(\text{nc} = 0\): the gradient w.r.t. nc is correct for every \(\text{nc} > 0\), but at exactly \(\text{nc} = 0\) it returns 0 rather than the true one-sided score $\tfrac12!\left(\tfrac{(x-\text{loc})/\text{scale}}{\text{df}}
  • 1\right)$. \(\text{nc} = 0\) is the boundary of the parameter domain (where the derivative is one-sided and the closed form has a removable singularity), so this measure-zero point is not special cased. Differentiate at a small \(\text{nc} > 0\) if the score at the null is needed.
  • Broadcasting: Supports JAX array broadcasting for all parameters.
  • Accuracy: inherits the ~1e-6 relative accuracy of ive for \(\lambda x \ge 4\); below that the series form is accurate to working precision.
  • Support boundary: for \(x \le \text{loc}\) the density is taken to be zero (logpdf returns -inf), matching scipy.stats.ncx2.pdf. At the single point \(x = \text{loc}\) the mathematical limit can diverge for \(\text{df} < 2\); that measure-zero point is reported as zero density here.

docs.title: pdf
docs.text:
pdf(x: ArrayLike, df: ArrayLike, nc: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Non-central chi-squared probability density function.

Computes the probability density function of the non-central chi-squared distribution with \(\text{df}\) degrees of freedom and non-centrality parameter \(\lambda\) (nc), in the location-scale family. This is exp(logpdf(...)); see logpdf for the full mathematical background, conventions, and differentiability notes.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• x: Quantile values. Scalar or array.
  • df: Degrees of freedom (must be positive). Scalar or array.
  • nc: Non-centrality parameter \(\lambda \ge 0\). Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location parameter (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale: Scale parameter (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Probability density values. Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numerax

# Single value
p = numerax.stats.ncx2.pdf(4.0, df=3.0, nc=2.0)

# Vectorized
x_vals = jnp.array([0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0])
ps = numerax.stats.ncx2.pdf(x_vals, df=3.0, nc=2.0)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Differentiable: w.r.t. x, nc, loc, and scale; differentiating w.r.t. df raises TypeError. The gradient w.r.t. nc returns 0 at exactly nc = 0 (a domain boundary). See logpdf for details.
  • Accuracy: inherits the ~1e-6 relative accuracy of ive.

docs.title: splitnorm
docs.text:
Split-normal distribution functions.

This module provides the density, distribution, and quantile functions of the split-normal (two-piece normal) distribution: a normal distribution with mode loc whose left and right halves have different scales. It is commonly used to describe asymmetric uncertainties. JAX and scipy do not provide it. The signatures follow the scipy.stats conventions, with the single scale replaced by scale_left and scale_right. The distribution functions are built on halfnorm, every function is evaluated in a form that stays accurate in both tails in float32 and float64, and all functions are compatible with JAX transformations (JIT, grad, vmap).

docs.title: cdf
docs.text:
cdf(x: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale_left: ArrayLike = 1, scale_right: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Split-normal cumulative distribution function.

Computes \(w_L\, S_h((\mu - x)/\sigma_L)\) below the mode, which keeps relative accuracy in the lower tail, and \(w_L + w_R\, F_h((x - \mu)/\sigma_R)\) above it, a sum of non-negative terms. See logpdf for the notation and mathematical background.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• x: Quantile values. Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location of the mode (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale_left: Scale below the mode (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.
  • scale_right: Scale above the mode (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Cumulative probabilities. Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: isf
docs.text:
isf(q: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale_left: ArrayLike = 1, scale_right: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Split-normal inverse survival function.

The mirror image of ppf: computes ppf(1 - q) without forming \(1 - q\) except in the lower tail (\(q > 1 - w_L/2\)), where it is exact, so upper-tail quantiles for tiny \(q\) and quantiles on the far side of a small \(w_R\) stay accurate. Returns inf at \(q = 0\), -inf at \(q = 1\), and nan outside \([0, 1]\). See logpdf for the notation and mathematical background.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• q: Survival probabilities in \([0, 1]\). Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location of the mode (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale_left: Scale below the mode (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.
  • scale_right: Scale above the mode (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Quantiles \(x\) where \(P(X > x) = q\). Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: logcdf
docs.text:
logcdf(x: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale_left: ArrayLike = 1, scale_right: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Split-normal log cumulative distribution function.

Below the mode, computes \(\log w_L + \log S_h((\mu - x)/\sigma_L)\) using halfnorm.logsf, which stays accurate far past where the CDF underflows. Above the mode, computes \(\text{log1p}(-w_R\, S_h((x - \mu)/\sigma_R))\) while the CDF exceeds \(1/2\) and \(\log(w_L + w_R\, F_h((x - \mu)/\sigma_R))\) otherwise, so that neither regime loses precision. See logpdf for the notation and mathematical background.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• x: Quantile values. Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location of the mode (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale_left: Scale below the mode (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.
  • scale_right: Scale above the mode (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Log cumulative probabilities. Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: logpdf
docs.text:
logpdf(x: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale_left: ArrayLike = 1, scale_right: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Split-normal log probability density function.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Computes the natural logarithm of the probability density function of the split-normal distribution, a normal distribution with mode loc whose two halves have separate scales.

docs.title: Mathematical Background
docs.text:
With mode \(\mu = \text{loc}\), left scale \(\sigma_L\) and right scale \(\sigma_R\), the density is

\[f(x) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\, \frac{1}{\sigma_L + \sigma_R} \begin{cases} e^{-(x - \mu)^2 / 2\sigma_L^2}, & x < \mu, \\ e^{-(x - \mu)^2 / 2\sigma_R^2}, & x \ge \mu, \end{cases}\]

which is continuous (with continuous derivative) at the mode. It reduces to \(N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) when \(\sigma_L = \sigma_R = \sigma\).

Equivalently, the split normal is a mixture of two half-normals with disjoint supports: with probability \(w_L = \sigma_L / (\sigma_L + \sigma_R)\), \(X = \mu - \sigma_L |Z|\), and with probability \(w_R = \sigma_R / (\sigma_L + \sigma_R)\), \(X = \mu + \sigma_R |Z|\). Writing \(F_h\) and \(S_h\) for the standard half-normal CDF and survival function, this gives

\[F(x) = \begin{cases} w_L\, S_h\!\left(\tfrac{\mu - x}{\sigma_L}\right), & x < \mu, \\ w_L + w_R\, F_h\!\left(\tfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma_R}\right), & x \ge \mu, \end{cases}\]

and the mirror image for \(S(x) = 1 - F(x)\). The quantile function is \(\mu - \sigma_L F_h^{-1}\!\left(\tfrac{w_L - q}{w_L}\right)\) for \(q < w_L\) and \(\mu + \sigma_R F_h^{-1}\!\left(\tfrac{q - w_L}{w_R} \right)\) otherwise, where \(F_h^{-1}(p) = \sqrt{2}\,\text{erfinv}(p) = -\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\tfrac{1 - p}{2}\right)\).

Every function in this module evaluates these in a form that is accurate in the relevant regime: tail probabilities are computed directly from the half-normal survival function (never as \(1 - \text{something}\)); logcdf and logsf use halfnorm.logsf on the side of the mode where they decay, so they stay accurate past where the probabilities underflow, and switch between \(\text{log1p}\) and a direct sum on the other side; the log-weights are evaluated as \(\log w_L = -\text{log1p}(\sigma_R/\sigma_L)\), accurate even when \(w_L\) is close to one; and ppf and isf, like halfnorm.ppf, use erfinv within the central half of each piece and \(\Phi^{-1}\) of the tail probability beyond it, so no regime loses precision to forming \(1 - q\).

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• x: Quantile values. Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location of the mode (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale_left: Scale below the mode (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.
  • scale_right: Scale above the mode (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Log probability density values. Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numerax

# A measurement of 3.0 with uncertainties -0.5 / +1.2
lp = numerax.stats.splitnorm.logpdf(3.4, loc=3.0, scale_left=0.5,
                                    scale_right=1.2)

# Vectorized
x_vals = jnp.array([-1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 5.0])
lps = numerax.stats.splitnorm.logpdf(x_vals, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0)

# Differentiable in x, loc, and both scales
grad_fn = jax.grad(numerax.stats.splitnorm.logpdf, argnums=(1, 2, 3))
d_loc, d_left, d_right = grad_fn(1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Differentiable: w.r.t. x, loc, scale_left and scale_right (and q for ppf/isf). Branch selections use safe substitutes so gradients stay NaN-free at finite points, including for extreme scale ratios. The density and its first derivative in x are continuous at the mode, and every function is continuous in all its arguments there, so first derivatives at the mode are two-sided. Second and higher derivatives in x jump at the mode; there the values for the side \(x \ge \mu\) are returned.
  • Precision: results follow the input dtype. Accuracy is close to machine precision in both float32 and float64; far in either tail pdf, cdf and sf are limited by the conditioning of \(e^{-y^2/2}\), about \(y^2\) ulps, as in halfnorm. Near \(q = w_L\) (ppf) or \(q = w_R\) (isf), the quantile is limited by the rounding of the weight itself.
  • Broadcasting: Supports JAX array broadcasting for all parameters.
  • Support: the whole real line. nan inputs propagate to nan.

docs.title: logsf
docs.text:
logsf(x: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale_left: ArrayLike = 1, scale_right: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Split-normal log survival function.

The mirror image of logcdf: above the mode, computes \(\log w_R + \log S_h((x - \mu)/\sigma_R)\) using halfnorm.logsf; below it, computes \(\text{log1p}(-w_L\, S_h((\mu - x)/\sigma_L))\) while the survival function exceeds \(1/2\) and \(\log(w_R + w_L\, F_h((\mu - x)/\sigma_L))\) otherwise. See logpdf for the notation and mathematical background.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• x: Quantile values. Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location of the mode (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale_left: Scale below the mode (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.
  • scale_right: Scale above the mode (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Log survival probabilities. Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: pdf
docs.text:
pdf(x: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale_left: ArrayLike = 1, scale_right: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Split-normal probability density function.

Computes \(\sqrt{2/\pi}\, e^{-y^2/2} / (\sigma_L + \sigma_R)\) for \(y = (x - \text{loc})/\sigma\), where \(\sigma\) is scale_left below the mode and scale_right above it. This is exp(logpdf(...)); see logpdf for the full mathematical background and conventions.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• x: Quantile values. Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location of the mode (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale_left: Scale below the mode (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.
  • scale_right: Scale above the mode (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Probability density values. Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: ppf
docs.text:
ppf(q: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale_left: ArrayLike = 1, scale_right: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Split-normal percent point function (inverse CDF).

Inverts the half-normal piece on the relevant side of the mode. In the central half of a piece (\(w_L/2 < q < w_L + w_R/2\)) it computes \(\mu + \sigma \sqrt{2}\, \text{erfinv}((q - w_L)/w)\), with \(\sigma\) and \(w\) the scale and weight of that side; in the lower tail \(\mu + \sigma_L \Phi^{-1}(q / 2w_L)\); and in the upper tail \(\mu - \sigma_R \Phi^{-1}((1 - q) / 2w_R)\), where \(1 - q\) is exact. Tiny \(q\), \(q\) close to one, and \(q\) on the far side of a small \(w_L\) all keep full precision. Returns -inf at \(q = 0\), inf at \(q = 1\), and nan outside \([0, 1]\). See logpdf for the notation and mathematical background.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• q: Probability values in \([0, 1]\). Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location of the mode (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale_left: Scale below the mode (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.
  • scale_right: Scale above the mode (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Quantiles \(x\) where \(P(X \leq x) = q\). Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: sf
docs.text:
sf(x: ArrayLike, loc: ArrayLike = 0, scale_left: ArrayLike = 1, scale_right: ArrayLike = 1) -> ArrayLike

Split-normal survival function (\(1 - \text{cdf}\)).

Computes \(w_R\, S_h((x - \mu)/\sigma_R)\) above the mode, which keeps relative accuracy in the upper tail, and \(w_R + w_L\, F_h((\mu - x)/\sigma_L)\) below it. See logpdf for the notation and mathematical background.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• x: Quantile values. Scalar or array.
  • loc: Location of the mode (default: 0). Scalar or array.
  • scale_left: Scale below the mode (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.
  • scale_right: Scale above the mode (must be positive, default: 1). Scalar or array.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Survival probabilities. Shape follows JAX broadcasting rules.

docs.title: numerax.utils
docs.text:
Utility functions for the numerax package.

This module provides development utilities for creating JAX-compatible functions and tools for working with PyTree structures, including parameter counting for machine learning models.

docs.title: count_params
docs.text:
count_params(pytree, filter=None, verbose=True)

Count the total number of parameters in a PyTree structure.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This function counts parameters in PyTree-based models by filtering for array-like objects and summing their sizes. It is particularly useful for neural network models built with JAX frameworks like Equinox.

The function traverses the PyTree structure, applies a filter to identify parameter arrays, and computes the total parameter count.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• pytree: The PyTree structure to count parameters in (e.g., a model, dict of arrays, or nested structure)
  • filter: Optional filter function to identify parameters. If None, uses equinox.is_array as the default filter. Custom filters should accept a single argument and return True for objects that should be counted
  • verbose: If True, prints the parameter count in scientific notation. If False, only returns the count silently

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: The total number of parameters as an integer

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • equinox: Install with pip install numerax[sciml] or pip install equinox

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import jax.numpy as jnp
from numerax.utils import count_params

# Simple dict-based model
model = {"weights": jnp.ones((10, 5)), "bias": jnp.zeros(5)}
count = count_params(model)
# Prints: Number of parameters: 5.5e+01
# Returns: 55

# With custom filter
count = count_params(
    model,
    filter=lambda x: hasattr(x, "ndim") and x.ndim > 1,
    verbose=False,
)
# Returns: 50 (only the weights matrix)

# With Equinox model
import equinox as eqx


class MLP(eqx.Module):
    layers: list

    def __init__(self, key):
        self.layers = [
            eqx.nn.Linear(10, 64, key=key),
            eqx.nn.Linear(64, 1, key=key),
        ]


model = MLP(jax.random.PRNGKey(0))
count = count_params(model)
# Counts all trainable parameters in the MLP

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The default filter (equinox.is_array) correctly identifies parameter arrays in Equinox modules and standard JAX PyTrees
  • For custom filtering logic, provide a function that returns True for leaves that should be counted as parameters
  • The function handles nested PyTree structures automatically

docs.title: preserve_metadata
docs.text:
preserve_metadata(decorator)

Wrapper that ensures a decorator preserves function metadata for documentation tools.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: When wrapping functions with decorators, metadata like __name__, __doc__, and __module__ can be lost if the decorator doesn't explicitly preserve them. This wrapper uses functools.wraps to ensure metadata is maintained, which is important for documentation generators like pdoc and for debugging.

docs.title: Args
docs.text: • decorator: The decorator function to wrap

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: A new decorator that preserves metadata

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from numerax.utils import preserve_metadata

# A simple decorator that doesn't preserve metadata
def my_decorator(func):
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper

# Without preserve_metadata, __doc__ and __name__ are lost
@my_decorator
def func1(x):
    """This docstring will be lost."""
    return x

# With preserve_metadata, they are preserved
@preserve_metadata(my_decorator)
def func2(x):
    """This docstring will be preserved."""
    return x

docs.title: tree_summary
docs.text:
tree_summary(pytree, is_leaf=None, max_depth=3, verbose=True, hide_empty=True)

Pretty-print PyTree structure with shapes and parameter counts.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This function displays a hierarchical view of a PyTree structure (e.g., neural network models) showing the organization, array shapes, data types, and parameter counts at each level. The output is similar to Keras' model.summary() or torchinfo's summaries. This is compatible with PyTree-based models from frameworks like Equinox.

docs.title: Args
docs.text:
• pytree: The PyTree structure to summarize (e.g., a model, dict of arrays, or nested structure)
  • is_leaf: Optional function to identify leaf nodes. If None, uses equinox.is_array as the default. Leaf nodes are displayed with shape, dtype, and parameter count details. Custom functions should accept a single argument and return True for leaves
  • max_depth: Maximum nesting depth to display. Nodes deeper than this level will not be shown. Defaults to 3
  • verbose: If True, prints the formatted summary. If False, only returns the total parameter count silently
  • hide_empty: If True, skips nodes with zero parameters. Defaults to True to avoid clutter from primitive attributes (integers, strings, functions) in neural network modules that don't contribute to parameter counts

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: The total number of parameters as an integer

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • equinox: Install with pip install numerax[sciml] or pip install equinox (required when using default is_leaf)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import jax.numpy as jnp
from numerax.utils import tree_summary

# Nested dict-based model
model = {
    "encoder": {
        "weights": jnp.ones((10, 20)),
        "bias": jnp.zeros(20),
    },
    "decoder": {
        "weights": jnp.ones((20, 5)),
        "bias": jnp.zeros(5),
    },
}

count = tree_summary(model)
# Prints formatted table showing structure
# Returns: 325

# With custom is_leaf function
tree_summary(model, is_leaf=lambda x: hasattr(x, "shape"))

# Limit depth
tree_summary(model, max_depth=2)

# Silent mode
count = tree_summary(model, verbose=False)
# Returns: 325 without printing

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Container nodes (dicts, lists, modules) show total parameter counts for their entire subtree
  • Leaf nodes (arrays) show shape, dtype, and individual param count
  • Indentation shows nesting depth in the PyTree structure
  • Works with Equinox modules, nested dicts, lists, tuples, and custom PyTree nodes
  • Use custom is_leaf functions to control what counts as a leaf node (useful for custom PyTree registrations)
